title: Orchestrated failover policy and KV-cache consistency workshop
summary: Deep technical workshop on multi-region routing, failover policies, and KV-cache consistency for Crescent's VPC deployment. Covered routing policies (latency, capacity, cost), per-region autoscale targets, graceful degradation to smaller quantized models, cache priming/eviction strategies, test playbooks for DR drills, and audit/KMS concerns. Agreed next steps include benchmarks, runbook draft, and failover simulation plan.
topics: batching and quantization tradeoffs during failover
next_steps: Redwood to run a 48h multi-region benchmark with Crescent's sample traffic (Mateo)
Crescent to share SSO/KMS contact and VPC peering details (Olivia)
Draft DR playbook#1 and share for review (Lena)
Schedule failover simulation window for mid-October (Samir + Lena)
Exchange cost model spreadsheet with quantized model vs full model comparisons (Mateo)
Security docs: SOC2 and encryption at rest/network links (Lena)
Set up a canary routing policy in staging that falls back to a <8B quantized model under latency SLO breaches (Priya)
action_items: Mateo Ruiz: run initial multi-region throughput/latency benchmark using Crescent sample traffic, produce CSV (due 2025-09-18)
Lena Park: draft DR playbook v0.1 including failback steps, contact points, and escalation matrix (due 2025-09-11)
Olivia Chan: send KMS/HSM contact details and compliance constraints re: key ownership (due 2025-09-10)
Samir Gupta: provision a staging VPC peering and test credentials for Redwood private control plane (due 2025-09-16)
Dana Lee: define SLOs (p50, p95 latency, and availability targets) and share monitoring endpoints (due 2025-09-12)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Mateo (Redwood SE), Samir, Dana, Olivia, Markus, Priya (Crescent)

[00:00] Lena: Okay everyone, thanks for carving time. The goal for today is to walk through a multi-region routing and DR playbook that fits Crescent's VPC constraints and high-sensitivity data needs. Mateo will run through the runtime and KV-cache implications.
[00:22] Mateo: Hi all — quick note, I'm going to call out some numbers and some assumptions. If anything's off please jump in.
[00:31] Samir: Great. We're primarily concerned about two scenarios: region outage and severe regional latency spikes. We want predictable behavior, minimal tail latency impact, and no data leakage cross-region.
[00:46] Mateo: Understood. We usually model two failure modes: hard outage where region is unreachable, and soft degradation where latency to a region increases beyond p95 threshold. Our routing policies support both.
[01:05] Dana: Can you explain how the routing policy actually decides where to send a request? Is it pure latency, or is capacity taken into account?
[01:16] Mateo: It's policy-driven. You can stack rules: prefer region by latency, then capacity, then cost. The routing engine evaluates recent p95 latency samples and active capacity. If a region lacks spare GPU slots to meet the request's concurrency int, it will deprioritize the region.
[01:36] Markus: "GPU slots" — are those per-model or per-queue? How do you account for KV cache locality?
[01:44] Mateo: Good question. Slots are capacity units in Redwood Dedicated pools. We pin model versions to a pool. The KV cache is per-pool and per-model shard. For low-latency you want cache hits local to the serving pool. Cross-region cache consistency is eventually consistent by default; we provide applications hooks to prime caches across regions during deployments.
[02:06] Olivia: That eventual consistency worries us. Financial workloads require strong controls. If a request fails over to another region, can the system ensure KV cache state is not stale in a way that violates correctness?
[02:20] Mateo: There's a couple patterns. Option A: synchronous replication for critical keys — we can configure a write-through/replicate mode for a small keyspace, but it adds write latency proportional to the cross-region RTT. Option B: accept eventual consistency and embed version checks in the application payload so the model can detect stale context and request a re-fetch. Option C: cache warming on failover — during failover we run a small priming job to populate the other region's KV with most-likely keys.
[02:50] Samir: How feasible is synchronous replication inside a VPC/on-prem setup? Will that require extra tunnels or special peering?
[02:59] Mateo: It depends. For Redwood Private with customer-managed networking you can set up direct VPC peering or use private interconnects. Synchronous replication requires low-latency links; otherwise the added latency kills the p50. If you can't guarantee that, we recommend selective sync only for the smallest critical keys.
[03:20] Priya: Can we get a sense of quantization tradeoffs when we degrade to smaller models during failover? E.g., 70B -> 7B quantized fallback — what's the latency and cost delta, and how much quality do we lose?
[03:33] Mateo: Rough numbers at our baseline: 70B float -> p95 latency 2200ms at seq len 256 on A100-ish hardware. 7B quantized (4-bit) -> p95 around 280ms, token cost ~1/8th. Quality loss depends on prompt complexity. For many structured-reply use cases, 7B is acceptable. For higher reasoning paths, you'll see regression. We recommend a canary set of eval prompts to measure acceptable degradation.
[03:59] Dana: Is the model switch atomic? If a region hits SLO breach and we route to a fallback model, do you keep state across models? KV cache keys keyed by model version?
[04:11] Mateo: We treat the cache namespace as model-versioned. When a failover uses a different model, the cache keys change namespace to avoid false hits. We also surface an optional cross-model mapping layer that translates or re-encode keys, but it's application work to ensure compatibility.
[04:29] Lena: Quick practical example: user traffic hits Region A, KV cache prime exists in A. If A goes down, we route to Region B where the model is a smaller quantized variant. How do we avoid a cold-start avalanche on B?
[04:44] Mateo: Two practices: (1) keep a small pre-warmed standby pool in B with hot cache primed for the top n keys; (2) apply rate smoothing — shed non-critical low-priority traffic for a window, prioritize authenticated/paid traffic. We can configure traffic classes so internal batch jobs are deprioritized.
[05:06] Samir: Pre-warmed standby — that costs money. We'll need a cost vs RTO analysis.
[05:11] Lena: Yes, which is why the team will run the benchmark and cost spreadsheet. Mateo, can you share a template?
[05:18] Mateo: I'll attach our cost-runner CSV. Links: Redwood benchmark template (note: internal link) — we'll push it to the shared drive.
[05:26] Olivia: Security question: when traffic routes cross regions, how do you control data residency and encryption keys? We need to make sure KMS keys never leave the EU.
[05:36] Mateo: For Redwood Private you can integrate your KMS/HSM so keys stay in the region. Key material never leaves your HSM. We support envelope encryption and customer-managed keys. For cross-region replication of encrypted payloads, you can use per-region keys and rotate accordingly. We'll include the detailed flow in security docs.
[05:55] Dana: Okay let me reframe: We want a playbook that defines: thresholds to trigger failover, who escalates, what model tier to fallback to, cache priming approach, and a rollback/fallthrough plan. Does Redwood have a playbook template?
[06:12] Lena: Yes, we have a DR playbook template. Mateo will help pr e-populate model-specific entries.
[06:20] Mateo: I'll put in recommended thresholds: p95 > 2x baseline for 3 consecutive 1-minute windows triggers soft-failover routing; complete region unreachability for 2 consecutive health-check intervals triggers hard outage failover.
[06:39] Samir: About traffic shaping — can Redwood tag traffic by customer tier and apply different failover policies? We want paid customers to keep higher-quality models while free-tier gets routed to quantized models.
[06:52] Mateo: Absolutely. We have token-level metadata and request-level attributes that permit tier-aware routing. You can also set per-API-key policies.
[07:02] Priya: On the KV cache consistency topic, do you support any CRDT-like merges?
[07:08] Mateo: Not as a built-in CRDT. The KV store is fast key-value with TTL and versioning. For CRDT behavior you need application-side logic or a synchronization service that we can interface with.
[07:22] Markus: For failover testing, what metrics should we capture to validate the playbook?
[07:29] Mateo: Capture p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput, cache hit ratio per-region, model inference errors, tail retries, and cold-start counts. Also audit logs for routing decisions and user-request IDs so you can replay flows.
[07:45] Olivia: Replay flows — can you replay in isolated staging without affecting production?
[07:49] Mateo: Yes, you can replay captures into a stage pool with traffic shaping. We can provide a replay harness that preserves headers and keys.
[07:59] Samir: Let's talk about failurefulimes — sorry, failure timelines. If Region A goes down, how long until failover completes? Is it seconds or minutes?
[08:10] Mateo: It depends on detection sensitivity, primed standby, and DNS TTLs. With an aggressive health-check and local router, typical soft-failover can start affecting traffic in 10-30 seconds. Hard failover with cache priming and model spin-up may take 60-180 seconds depending on warm pools.
[08:29] Dana: We need deterministic behavior. Those ranges are a bit wide. Can we lock to an RTO of 90s for critical endpoints?
[08:37] Lena: We can aim for that with pre-warmed pools and aggressive health checks; cost will be higher. Mateo, can we show a configuration that targets 90s RTO in the runbook?
[08:46] Mateo: Yes; I'll include an RTO vs cost table.
[08:51] Priya: About model quantization — are there recommended quant profiles per architecture? Like Q4_0, Q4_1, INT8?
[08:59] Mateo: For Llama-like architectures we often recommend 4-bit quant (Q4_0) for 7B and 13B models. For 70B, Q4_1 or 8-bit is safer to retain quality. We also recommend mixed precision for KV-cache heavy workloads to avoid numerical drift.
[09:19] Samir: Mixed precision — does that complicate GPU scheduling or require special kernels?
[09:24] Mateo: It does require runtime kernel selection. Our serving engine picks kernels per-layer and per-dtype at runtime, but we prefer pinned configs for predictable performance.
[09:34] Lena: (interrupting) There was a question in the thread earlier about trace IDs and how we correlate request traces across regions. Mateo?
[09:39] Mateo: We inject a global request ID at the edge. Our tracing pipeline supports cross-region span stitching so you can see a single request across services and regions. We'll include sample logs in the replay.
[09:48] Dana: On the playbook's steps during a failover, who is the primary responsible party on the Redwood side? Is it the SE on-call?
[09:55] Lena: Operationally, Redwood support handles initial triage; for deeper remediation the SE on-call and the customer's infra lead coordinate. We'll include an escalation matrix with contact info.
[10:06] Samir: What about operator mistakes during a failover? We want an automated rollback path if someone flips something incorrectly.
[10:15] Mateo: We support automated guardrails: route changes require signed change requests in prod via the console or API with role-based approvals. For emergency failovers you can have a break-glass route but it records an audit entry and triggers a postmortem workflow.
[10:31] Priya: Let's go through a scenario: A large traffic spike originates in EU region, saturates EU pool. Routing rules attempt to spill into US West. But US West has limited pre-warmed capacity; the first requests to US West cause cache miss storms. Walk me through mitigation.
[10:49] Mateo: Steps: (1) rate limit spillover and apply token-bucket to cap bursting; (2) route only a fraction of requests to US West while progressively ramping; (3) activate cache warming jobs that fetch top session keys; (4) degrade non-essential model features to conserve capacity (e.g., long-context windows).
[11:12] Dana: How do you implement cache warming at scale? If we have tens of millions of keys, you can't pre-warm all.
[11:20] Mateo: Correct. We prioritize top n keys by access frequency and session affinity. For new sessions we rely on on-demand fetches with backpressure. We also support probabilistic prefetch where you pre-warm keys for a sample of users.
[11:33] Samir: Will the benchmark exercise show cache-hit changes and cold-start counts?
[11:36] Mateo: Yes, we'll instrument that.
[11:38] Lena: Quick interjection: there may be some transcription artifacts—ignore 'K V cash' in earlier notes, it's KV cache.
[11:44] (laughter)
[11:48] Olivia: About compliance, if we have cross-region failover, we need proof that data from EU accounts never lands on US storage. How is that enforced?
[11:58] Mateo: Two layers: (1) routing policy with residency constraints — you can mark certain tenants as region-locked so they never leave EU; (2) for global tenants, you can restrict only anonymized payloads to cross-region. We'll show configuration examples.
[12:14] Priya: For region-locked tenants, what's the fallback if the region is down? Do we LTC — live transfer to another region? Or do we return 503s?
[12:24] Mateo: For region-locked, by definition you can't move the payload. Options: return a 503 and surface a degraded mode (e.g., read-only cached responses), or failover to a replica inside the same data center if you have on-prem options. Many customers elect to return a graceful fallback for strict residency.
[12:39] Samir: We prefer 503 + queued retry versus risking residency violation.
[12:44] Lena: Noted. Mateo, please add that as a recommended policy in playbook v0.1.
[12:50] Mateo: Will do.
[12:52] Samir: Can we talk about monitoring and alerting thresholds? For instance, do we alert on cache hit ratio drops or only on latency?
[12:59] Mateo: Both. We recommend a composite alert: e.g., p95 latency > threshold AND cache hit ratio drop > 10% triggers a severity-2. Single-metric alerts for p99 or error-rate are also important.
[13:14] Dana: Re: batch endpoints — can we shift large batch jobs during failover to low-priority pools?
[13:20] Mateo: Yes. We have routing tags that mark batch vs interactive traffic. During failover, batch jobs are deprioritized or replayed off-peak.
[13:28] Priya: About the DR drill — what does a simulated outage look like? Do you do DNS-level cuts or router-level blackholes?
[13:36] Mateo: We recommend router-level blackholes for realism: disable health checks for a region so the router marks it unhealthy. That simulates sudden outage while preserving DNS. It lets you test cache warming and failover without changing DNS propagation.
[13:50] Samir: How often do customers do these drills? Quarterly? Semi-annually?
[13:55] Lena: Depends on criticality. For high-financial-impact customers, quarterly is common. We'll capture cadence in the playbook.
[14:04] Markus: Are there real-world examples you've seen where cache priming failed? What were lessons learned?
[14:10] Mateo: One case: a customer over-primed keys and exhausted memory in standby pools. Lesson: limit pre-warming to top percentile and use eviction TTLs. Another: priming used stale keys leading to incorrect outputs — ensure versioning and sequence numbers are validated.
[14:29] Olivia: Can we have a brief walkthrough of the runbook steps? Maybe 8-10 bullet points?
[14:36] Lena: Sure, Mateo will read a condensed flow; then we'll align owners.
[14:40] Mateo: Runbook (condensed): 1) Detect: composite alert triggers. 2) Triage: check region health, cache hit ratio, queue depth. 3) Activate spill routing to standby region with rate limiting. 4) Prime cache for top keys in standby. 5) Monitor latencies and errors; if above thresholds, escalate to on-call. 6) If rollback needed, restore routing to orig region when healthy. 7) Postmortem and update playbook.
[15:03] Samir: Who performs step 4 — Redwood or Crescent?
[15:07] Mateo: It can be automated by Redwood in Private setups if you provide credentials. Alternatively, Crescent can run warming jobs using our SDK. We'll make both options available in the runbook.
[15:18] Priya: Will we see examples in the runbook of the API calls?
[15:22] Mateo: Yes, sample curl/SDK commands for cache write, priming, and routing changes.
[15:28] Olivia: Quick security check — all routing changes must be audited and encrypted in transit.
[15:33] Mateo: Confirmed. All API calls use mTLS or API keys over TLS, and every change is logged with a trace id.
[15:40] Dana: About autoscaling: if we add capacity in another region during failover, how long for instances to come up?
[15:48] Mateo: GPU instance spin-up times vary; with pre-baked images and standby capacity it can be 45-90s. If you need faster, maintain a hot standby.
[15:57] Lena: Earlier we mentioned per-route dashboards — can we show how to annotate routes with SLO targets and cost budgets?
[16:05] Mateo: Yes, the Console supports per-route annotations: latency SLO, cost cap, and failover policy. We'll include screenshots in the follow-up deck.
[16:15] Samir: For the benchmark, what data do you need from us?
[16:19] Mateo: Sample traffic capture (anonymized), typical session distribution, top prompt templates, and desired SLOs. Also model preference list and any pinned versions.
[16:29] Dana: We'll share a 1-hour day-in-the-life capture and a shorter spike trace.
[16:33] Lena: Great. Now, quick deep-dive on batching behavior during failover: Mateo?
[16:37] Mateo: Batching helps throughput but adds latency. During failover you want to reduce batch windows to favor latency. Our runtime can adapt batch size based on load: when throughput drops it widens batch windows for efficiency, but in failover we can override to cap batch size to maintain latency SLOs. There's also continuous batching for streaming responses — we carefully tune so streaming tokens aren't delayed.
[17:02] Priya: Does changing batch windows require model reloads?
[17:06] Mateo: No, it's a runtime parameter. However, aggressive batching can hurt real-time properties for chat. We expose per-route batch policies.
[17:13] Samir: About telemetry — will we get per-request token-level timing to debug slow tokens?
[17:20] Mateo: Yes, you can enable token-level timing traces for a sample of requests. It increases overhead but is invaluable for root-cause analysis.
[17:29] Olivia: For on-prem options, if we have air-gapped data centers, is the Redwood control plane still required?
[17:37] Mateo: For fully air-gapped, Redwood offers an on-prem control plane package with optional sync windows. For private deployments inside a VPC but with outbound to Redwood control plane, we can do hybrid. We'll lay out options in the deployment appendix.
[17:51] Priya: Regarding failback — after region recovers, do you prefer gradual ramp vs instant cutback?
[17:58] Mateo: Gradual ramp is safer — a canary ratio to shift traffic back while monitoring. Instant cutback risks thrash and cache storms. The playbook will recommend a staged rollback with health gates.
[18:12] Samir: If we maintain per-region model versions, how do we handle version skew during failback if different regions ran different quantized versions?
[18:23] Mateo: We version keys by model build id. On failback, either you do a compatibility migration for critical keys or you invalidate and rebuild. We'll recommend a schema for key versions to make migrations tractable.
[18:38] Lena: Time check — we're ~18 minutes in. Let's open for questions and prioritize the action items.
[18:45] (brief pause)
[18:48] Dana: I want to reiterate: any cross-region test must be cleared with legal and security first. We'll need a sign-off matrix.
[18:56] Olivia: I'll produce the sign-off checklist.
[18:59] Priya: One last question: does Redwood support synthetic traffic injection to test failover?
[19:05] Mateo: Yes, we have an injection harness that can run spike profiles and simulate region blackholes. We'll include it in the benchmark runbook.
[19:14] Samir: Perfect. Can you commit to producing the initial benchmark and playbook draft in the next two weeks?
[19:20] Lena: Yes — we'll own that cadence. Mateo will run the benchmark; I'll draft the playbook and security appendix.
[19:27] Markus: Any more deep implementation details we should capture now? I want to know the storage layer for KV — is it Redis, RocksDB, custom in-memory?
[19:36] Mateo: It's a sharded in-memory store backed by RocksDB for persistence. Evictions use an LRU with configurable TTLs. We'll include architecture diagrams.
[19:48] Priya: Mixed-precision kernel selection — could we absorb some of that complexity? Is there an API to lock kernels so behavior is deterministic across regions?
[19:58] Mateo: You can pin kernel profiles per-deployment. We surface a kernel policy in the deployment config. Good idea to include recommended profiles in the playbook.
[20:09] Samir: Let's close with a recap and owners.
[20:12] Lena: Recap: Redwood runs benchmark (Mateo), draft playbook + security appendix (Lena), Crescent provides traffic captures + SLOs + VPC info (Samir/Olivia), schedule drill in mid-Oct (Samir + Lena). Action items and owners captured in the doc.
[20:30] Samir: Thanks everyone. Good session.
[20:33] Lena: We'll follow up with the deck, runbook draft, and the benchmark template.
[20:38] Mateo: I'll upload the benchmark script and a sample CSV.
[20:41] (call ends)

Notes about transcription: occasional ASR errors: "K V cash" should read "KV cache"; "quantize-ation" artifacts present in raw transcript. Some speaker labels may be simplified.
